title: Esther 7:7–10
context: Esther 7:7–10 records Haman’s end. The king rises in anger and goes into the palace garden. Haman stays to plead with Esther for his life and falls on the couch where she is reclining. When the king returns, he takes this as an assault on the queen, and Haman’s face is covered. Harbonah, one of the eunuchs, mentions the gallows fifty cubits high that Haman built for Mordecai, and the king orders Haman hanged on it. A cubit was about 18 inches. The word translated gallows may refer to a tall stake or pole, and interpreters describe the method of execution in different ways. Haman is executed on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king’s anger subsides. The text reports the death briefly and without comment. Both traditions read it soberly as a just reversal, in which the evil Haman planned falls on himself (compare Psalm 7:15–16), without gloating over his death.

verses.text: The king arose in his wrath from the banquet of wine and went into the palace garden. Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen, for he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The king rises in anger and goes into the garden, and Haman stays to beg Esther for his life, seeing that the king has determined evil against him. Arminian readers see the man who showed no mercy now pleading for it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the irony of Haman begging a Jewish woman for his life. Both traditions read the verse soberly, without gloating, as part of the story’s reversal.

verses.text: Then the king returned out of the palace garden into the place of the banquet of wine; and Haman had fallen on the couch where Esther was. Then the king said, “Will he even assault the queen in front of me in the house?” As the word went out of the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face.
verses.arminianNotes: The king returns to find Haman fallen on Esther’s couch, takes it as an assault on the queen, and Haman’s face is covered. Arminians see Haman’s desperate act sealing his fate, though the text does not say he meant harm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the covering of Haman’s face as a sign of condemnation. Both traditions note that the narrator records the scene briefly, and they avoid elaborating on it.

verses.text: Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs who were with the king, said, “Behold, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman has made for Mordecai, who spoke good for the king, is standing at Haman’s house.” The king said, “Hang him on it!”
verses.arminianNotes: Harbonah mentions the gallows fifty cubits high that Haman built for Mordecai, and the king orders Haman hanged on it. A cubit was about 18 inches. Arminian readers see the instrument of Haman’s plan turned against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversal as fitting justice. Both traditions note that Harbonah describes Mordecai as one who spoke good for the king, which recalls 6:2, and they read the verse soberly.

verses.text: So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the king’s wrath was pacified.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman is hanged on the gallows he prepared for Mordecai, and the king’s anger subsides. Arminians read the brief account as just retribution, the evil a man planned for another falling on himself (compare Psalm 7:15–16).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice in the reversal, though the book does not name him. Both traditions read the verse soberly, without gloating, and note that the threat to the Jews is not yet removed, as chapter 8 shows.
